title: Disney Park Etiquette: The Unwritten Rules
h1: Disney Park Etiquette: The Unwritten Rules
metaDescription: Stroller parking, line-cutting, ECV courtesy, kids on shoulders, flash photography and who to tip — the unwritten rules of a Disney park, stated plainly.
summary: The conventions nobody explains at the gate: queue behaviour, stroller and mobility device courtesy, photography, viewing spots, and a straight answer on tipping at both resorts.
intro: A Disney park is one of the densest public spaces most people ever spend a day in — sixty thousand strangers sharing walkways, queues, and sightlines for fourteen hours in the heat. Almost every unpleasant interaction you will witness comes from someone not knowing a convention rather than from someone being deliberately awful. The conventions are learnable, and they take about ten minutes.

This page covers them plainly, including the ones that will make you slightly less comfortable to read: yes, sending one person to hold a place in a queue for five people is line-cutting; yes, putting a child on your shoulders during a parade ruins the view for everyone behind you; and yes, you tip your server the same way you would anywhere else, because they are paid the same way servers are paid anywhere else.

The organising principle is simple. In a space this crowded, the cost of your convenience is almost always paid by a stranger you will never see again. Most etiquette here is just noticing who that stranger is.
keyPoints: Enter a queue with your entire party. Sending one person ahead to hold places is line-cutting, however you frame it.
Park your stroller where Cast Members direct, tag it clearly, and never leave anything valuable in it.
Mobility device courtesy runs both ways: drive slowly and announce yourself, and do not step in front of a moving ECV.
Flash photography is prohibited on dark rides and in theatres. It ruins the effect for everyone in the room.
Do not put a child on your shoulders at a parade or nighttime show. Sit on the kerb or move to the back.
Tip your table-service server 18 to 20 per cent, your bartender per drink, and housekeeping a few dollars a night. Most other Cast Members cannot accept tips.
Pull to the side before you stop walking. The single most common cause of collisions at both resorts is someone stopping dead in a walkway.

sections.heading: Queues: line-cutting and party-joining
body: Enter the queue with everyone who is going to ride. That is the whole rule, and every dispute you will ever see in a Disney line comes from someone bending it. Sending one person in at the start while four others shop and then join them at the merge point is line-cutting, and the fact that it is common does not make it acceptable to the eighty people it pushes back.

There are genuine exceptions and Cast Members apply them sensibly. A parent taking a child to the bathroom mid-queue and rejoining is fine — that is what Attraction Queue Return exists for, and telling the Cast Member at the entrance before you go makes it official. One person catching up with a group of two is not going to trouble anybody. A party of six joining one person forty minutes in is a different thing entirely and everybody around you knows it.

If it happens near you, tell a Cast Member rather than confronting the group. Queue confrontations escalate faster than any other conflict in a theme park, they happen in front of children, and they never end with the queue-jumpers leaving. A quiet word to the Cast Member at the merge point is more effective and costs you nothing.

Two smaller conventions. Keep up with the line rather than leaving a twenty-foot gap while you scroll — the gap makes the queue look longer than it is and everybody behind you notices. And do not let children run ahead through switchbacks; it is unsafe, and a child weaving through a crowd at knee height is how people get knocked over.

items: Join the queue with your whole party. If someone is not there yet, wait outside.
If you must leave mid-queue, tell a Cast Member at the entrance and use the queue return accommodation.
Keep up with the person in front. Large gaps make the line look longer and slow everybody down.
Do not save places for a group that is shopping or eating elsewhere.
Report line-cutting to a Cast Member rather than confronting people. Confrontations in queues never end well.
Do not let children run through switchbacks. It is unsafe and it is how strangers get hurt.

callout.title: What Cast Members can and cannot do
callout.body: A Cast Member at a queue merge point can and will manage a group that is joining a line improperly, and they are trained to do it without a confrontation. What they cannot do is change a policy, make an exception on a height requirement, or override a Lightning Lane return window. Asking them to puts a person on minimum patience in an impossible position, and the answer will still be no.

sections.heading: Stroller parking
body: Park where you are directed, in the rows, wheels facing the same way as everyone else's. Cast Members organise stroller parking constantly because a disorganised stroller row blocks a walkway that thousands of people need, and if yours is parked badly they will move it. That is not rudeness; it is the job.

Expect your stroller to be moved even if you parked it perfectly. Rows get reorganised, areas get cleared for parades, and a stroller left in one spot at 11 AM is routinely in a different row at 1 PM. This is exactly why you should tag it — a bright ribbon, a luggage tag, a strip of patterned tape — because a Disney park at midday contains several hundred identical strollers in identical colours.

Never leave anything valuable in a parked stroller. Phones, wallets, cameras, and tablets all disappear, and the parks are not a special exception to how the world works. Rain covers, snacks, and a spare shirt are fine. Everything else comes with you.

Two things people do that make everybody's day worse: parking across a walkway or an emergency exit path because the proper row was full, and using a stroller as a battering ram through a crowd. If the row is full, ask a Cast Member where the overflow is. If the crowd is dense, wait rather than push — a stroller at ankle height is a genuine injury risk and the person you hit will not see it coming.

callout.title: Tag it, photograph it
callout.body: Tie something distinctive to the handle and take a photograph of the stroller with the tag visible before you walk away. If it has been moved, showing the photo to a Cast Member at the attraction turns a fifteen-minute hunt into a thirty-second one. Experienced parents do this on day one and never think about it again.

sections.heading: ECV and wheelchair courtesy, in both directions
body: This section is deliberately two-sided, because most guidance on it only addresses one party and that is why the friction persists.

If you are driving a mobility device: go slowly in crowds, and slower than you think is necessary. Announce yourself before moving through a tight space rather than nudging. Do not tailgate the person in front; they cannot see you and they are about to stop suddenly, because everyone in a Disney park stops suddenly. Park clear of walkways and queue entrances. And take the time to learn the controls before the crowds build — the first hour of the morning is a much better place to discover an ECV's turning circle than the middle of Main Street at parade time.

If you are walking: do not step in front of a moving ECV or wheelchair. They cannot stop as fast as you can and the person driving has less visibility than you assume. Do not let children dart across in front of one. Do not lean on someone's chair, move it, or push it without being asked — a wheelchair is a person's body in this context, not furniture. And do not occupy accessible viewing areas at parades and shows if you do not need them; those areas are small and they are the only option for the people they exist for.

One thing worth saying to both groups: the vast majority of people using a mobility device at a Disney park are there because ten miles a day is not possible for them, not because they are gaming a system. There is no system left to game — queues at both resorts are mainstreamed, and using a wheelchair does not get anyone a shorter line.

items: Drivers: slow in crowds, announce before moving, no tailgating, park clear of walkways.
Drivers: practise in the first quiet hour of the morning, not in the parade crowd.
Walkers: never step in front of a moving device, and keep children from darting across.
Walkers: do not touch, lean on, or move someone's chair. Ask before you help with anything.
Everyone: leave accessible viewing areas to the people who need them.
Everyone: on a bus with a lift, wheelchair users board first and you wait. This is not queue-jumping.

sections.heading: Photography, flash, and phones
body: Flash photography is prohibited on dark rides and inside theatres at both resorts. This is not a suggestion — a flash inside Pirates of the Caribbean or the Haunted Mansion destroys the illusion for every other person in that room, and on some attractions it can distract the operators. Turn it off before you board, because you will not be able to find the setting in the dark.

The same applies to screen brightness. A phone at full brightness held up for four minutes in a dark ride is a light source, and everybody behind you is watching your screen instead of the show. If you are filming, turn the brightness down and hold it low.
Selfie sticks are prohibited at both resorts and refused at security. Tripods that do not fit in a bag are refused. Drones are prohibited across both properties entirely.

On people: do not photograph other people's children, and do not photograph Cast Members without asking, particularly the ones performing. PhotoPass photographers are happy to take a shot on your own phone as well as the official one, which is a small courtesy they extend constantly and nobody asks for. And if you are setting up a family photo in a walkway, step to the side first — the castle is not going anywhere and the four hundred people behind you are trying to get to Fantasyland.

callout.title: The one that genuinely matters
callout.body: Flash on a dark ride is the single most common etiquette failure at both resorts and the one with the widest impact — one flash affects everybody in a whole show scene. Disable it at the start of the day rather than per-ride. If your phone fires it automatically in low light, find the setting now, at home, rather than in a Doom Buggy.

sections.heading: Parades, shows, and kids on shoulders
body: Do not put a child on your shoulders at a parade or a nighttime show. It is the etiquette failure people defend most and it is the least defensible: a child on shoulders is roughly six and a half feet of solid obstruction, and everybody in the fifteen or twenty people directly behind you loses the thing they waited an hour for. If your child cannot see, move to the front kerb, not upward.

At parades, the convention at both resorts is that people sit on the kerb at the front and stand behind them. If you arrive late, stand at the back — do not walk to the front and stand in front of families who have been sitting there for forty minutes. If you are sitting, keep children's legs out of the route.

Do not rope off territory. Blankets, folding chairs, and a single family member holding a twelve-foot stretch of kerb for a group who are still eating dinner are all outside the convention, and at busy shows Cast Members will ask you to consolidate. Save a space for the people who are actually there.

In theatres, fill in toward the middle of the row rather than sitting on the aisle and making forty people climb past you. Cast Members will ask you to move down and it is faster if they do not have to. And do not talk through shows — it seems obvious and it is the most common complaint at every theatre attraction at both resorts.

items: No children on shoulders at parades or nighttime shows. Move forward, not upward.
Sit at the front kerb, stand behind. Do not arrive late and stand in front of seated families.
Do not reserve large areas with blankets or chairs for people who are elsewhere.
Fill in toward the middle of a theatre row instead of blocking the aisle seat.
Do not talk through shows. The audience around you can hear every word.
When a show ends, keep moving. Stopping in the middle of an exiting crowd of ten thousand people is how crushes start.

sections.heading: Walkways and moving through crowds
body: Pull to the side before you stop. This one convention prevents more collisions than everything else on this page combined. Both resorts fill their walkways with people looking at phones, and a family stopping dead in the middle of a thoroughfare to consult the app produces a pile-up behind them within seconds.

Do not walk eight abreast. A large group spread across the full width of a walkway makes it impossible for anybody to pass, and on a busy evening that is genuinely the difference between a crowd flowing and a crowd stalling. Pair up.

Look before you back up, particularly with a stroller, and particularly at the bottom of a ride exit ramp — that is the highest-collision spot in any Disney park. And be aware of what is behind and below you: children, wheelchairs, and small strollers are all outside the eyeline of an adult scanning a map.

Smoking and vaping are permitted only in designated areas, which at both resorts are outside the park gates. There is no smoking anywhere inside any of the six parks, and vaping is treated identically.

sections.heading: Tipping: a straight answer
body: Table-service servers at both resorts are tipped employees paid on the same model as servers anywhere else in the US, and the convention is 18 to 20 per cent of the pre-discount total. That applies at buffets and family-style restaurants too, where a server is still bringing drinks, clearing plates, and managing your table — the food arriving on a counter does not change how that person is paid.

Most other Cast Members cannot accept tips at all, and offering puts them in an awkward position. Ride operators, PhotoPass photographers, shop staff, and character attendants are not tipped positions. The tipped roles are the hospitality ones: servers, bartenders, bell services, valet, housekeeping, and transport drivers.
Large parties should check the bill. Both resorts add an automatic gratuity for parties above a certain size at most table-service restaurants, and it is easy to tip twice by accident.
For a family on a week-long trip, tipping is a real line in the budget rather than a rounding error. Work it into what you plan to spend on food rather than discovering it on day three.

callout.title: Check for the automatic gratuity
callout.body: Parties above a certain size have a service charge added automatically at most table-service restaurants at both resorts, and prix-fixe and character dining experiences frequently include it too. Read the bill before you add anything. Tipping twice is common, it is expensive across a week, and nobody will point it out to you.

sections.heading: How to treat Cast Members
body: The person in front of you did not set the policy, cannot change it, and has already been asked today. That is the entire brief. Cast Members at both resorts have close to zero discretion over height requirements, Lightning Lane return windows, capacity closures, and refunds, and pressing them for an exception is asking someone on a hot pavement to do something they are not permitted to do.

What they can do is often more useful than what you were going to ask for. Cast Members can arrange queue re-entry, find you a quieter seat, sort out a broken stroller, get an allergy coordinator, locate first aid, redirect you to a shorter line, and solve a startling number of problems if you describe the problem rather than demanding a specific solution. Lead with what has gone wrong, not with what you want.

Both resorts run a compliment system, and it genuinely reaches people. If someone helps you, get their name and mention it at Guest Relations or in the app. It takes two minutes and it counts for something in their record — which is more than a tip they are not allowed to accept would do.

sections.heading: The short version
body: If you remember nothing else from this page, these are the ten things that account for nearly all of the friction in a Disney park. None of them cost you anything and every one of them makes somebody else's day better.
The underlying test is simple: before you do the convenient thing, work out who pays for it. If the answer is a stranger who cannot object, do the other thing.

items: Join the queue with your whole party.
Pull to the side before you stop walking.
Turn your flash off at the start of the day and leave it off.
No children on shoulders at parades or nighttime shows.
Park your stroller where directed, tag it, and leave nothing valuable in it.
Never step in front of a moving ECV, and never move someone's wheelchair.
Tip your server 18 to 20 per cent, and check whether it is already on the bill.
Fill in toward the middle of theatre rows and stop talking when the show starts.
Leave accessible viewing areas for people who need them.
Ask Cast Members for help with problems, not for exceptions to policies.

faqs.q: Is it line-cutting if my family joins me partway through a queue?
faqs.a: Yes, if it is a group joining one person. The convention at both resorts is that you enter the queue with everyone who is riding. A single person catching up with a small group is not going to trouble anyone; a party of six joining one person forty minutes in is line-cutting, and everybody standing behind them knows it.

faqs.q: Can I put my child on my shoulders to watch the parade?
faqs.a: Please do not. A child on shoulders is around six and a half feet of solid obstruction and it costs the view for fifteen or twenty people directly behind you, most of whom waited longer than you did. If your child cannot see, move to the front kerb or move to the back — move forward, not upward.

faqs.q: Do I tip at Disney restaurants?
faqs.a: At table service, yes — 18 to 20 per cent, the same as anywhere else in the US, and that includes buffets and family-style meals where a server is still working your table. Check the bill first, because parties above a certain size and most prix-fixe experiences have a gratuity added automatically.

faqs.q: Can I tip a Cast Member who helped me?
faqs.a: Most Cast Members cannot accept tips, including ride operators, photographers, shop staff and character attendants. Offering puts them in an awkward position. What genuinely helps is getting their name and passing a compliment to Guest Relations or through the app — it reaches their record and it counts for something.

faqs.q: Why is flash photography banned on dark rides?
faqs.a: Because one flash affects everybody in the show scene, not just the person taking the photo. It destroys the illusion the room is built to create and on some attractions it can distract the operators. Disable flash at the start of your day rather than trying to find the setting in the dark on a moving ride vehicle.

faqs.q: Where should I park my stroller?
faqs.a: In the marked rows, facing the same way as the others, and never across a walkway or an emergency exit path. Expect Cast Members to move it as rows get reorganised, so tag it with something distinctive and photograph it before you walk away. Take anything valuable with you.

faqs.q: Someone is being rude in the queue. What should I do?
faqs.a: Tell a Cast Member rather than confronting them. Queue confrontations escalate faster than any other conflict in a theme park, they happen in front of children, and they almost never result in the other party leaving. A quiet word at the merge point is more effective and costs you nothing.
